    OpenJDK / Linux ThreadMXBean: remove /proc parsing from current-thread user CPU time
    Kernel-facing hotspot with cloned local source plus published before/after profile evidence.
    CPUKernel/JVMPublished proof40x lower latency
    Source Repository and Local Files

    Repository: openjdk/jdk
    Local source: C:/VoxxedDays/GitRepos/openjdk-jdk/src/hotspot/os/linux/os_linux.cpp and C:/VoxxedDays/GitRepos/openjdk-jdk/test/micro/org/openjdk/bench/vm/runtime/ThreadMXBeanBench.java

    Upstream Trail
    QuestDB articleOriginal bug reportOpenJDK repositoryLocal cloned repo: C:/VoxxedDays/GitRepos/openjdk-jdk
    PR / Functional Summary

    The old Linux path for current-thread user CPU time opened /proc/self/task/<tid>/stat, read kernel-generated text, searched backward for the last right parenthesis to survive hostile command names, parsed thirteen fields with sscanf, and only then converted clock ticks to nanoseconds. The new path instead uses pthread_getcpuclockid plus a low-bit flip to CPUCLOCK_VIRT and reads the time through clock_gettime.

    QuestDB article and cited commit 858d2e434ddOpenJDK repository

    Commit validation: The local clone clearly contains the post-fix Linux hotspot code and the JMH benchmark file. The exact upstream commit hash 858d2e434dd is cited by the QuestDB article, but that specific revision is not present in the shallow local clone, so the code-to-commit mapping here is local-source-validated and article-backed rather than locally commit-checked out.

    Functional explanation: The API still reports current-thread user CPU time. The optimization changes only how that value is retrieved on Linux: instead of opening and parsing procfs task-stat text, it asks the kernel for a CPU clock id, flips the low clock-type bits to VIRT, and reads the result through clock_gettime.

    Why 10%+ is plausible: This is far beyond the 10% bar. The published benchmark moves from 11.186 us/op to 0.279 us/op under 16 threads, roughly 40x lower latency. That directly removes extra syscalls, VFS work, kernel-side string formatting, userspace parsing, and close-path locking overhead.

    Flamegraph Proof

    This point uses the QuestDB article's published before/after CPU profiles and benchmark numbers. The OpenJDK source is cloned locally for code validation, but a full local JDK rebuild and rerun was not executed in this workspace, so this proof is explicitly published-evidence-backed rather than locally regenerated.

    Published timing: before 11.186 us/op, after 0.279 us/op, delta 10.907 us/op and about 97.51% lower latency.

    Before vs after slowdown: the old procfs path is about 40.1x slower, which is roughly 3909% slower than the fixed path.

    Visual hotspot share in this partial: the expensive procfs branch occupies about 90.7% of the simplified active bar before the change, versus about 72.2% for the clock-based branch after it, a 18.5 point drop.

    What the flamegraph proves: before, most of the width is open/read/parse/close control flow; after, the wide block collapses into one clock query plus small JVM glue. Functionally the API is unchanged. Technically the kernel-facing work shrinks from a procfs round-trip to a direct CPU-clock read.

    Before profile, published

    QuestDB article: multiple syscalls, procfs formatting, userspace parsing, and close-path futex/locking activity dominate.

    After profile, published

    QuestDB article: the path collapses to one clock_gettime syscall plus JVM-side framing; no procfs open/read/parse path remains.

    Prediction Signal

    Before signal: multiple syscalls plus procfs synthesis and userspace text parsing for every metric read. After direction: direct kernel CPU-clock query with no file I/O and no sscanf. Predicted trace: span=threadmxbean.usercpu top=open,read,sscanf,close -> clock_gettime.

    Full Code Example With Inline uOps and mWh

    These uOps and mWh annotations are illustrative talk aids, not direct hardware measurements.

    static bool get_thread_clockid(Thread* thread, clockid_t* clockid, bool total) {
    constexpr clockid_t CLOCK_TYPE_MASK = 3;
    constexpr clockid_t CPUCLOCK_VIRT = 1;
    int rc = pthread_getcpuclockid(thread->osthread()->pthread_id(), clockid);
    // One direct kernel query replaces open/read/parse/close control flow. | ~35 uOps + syscall framing | lower kernel work than /proc path
    if (!total) {
        *clockid = (*clockid & ~CLOCK_TYPE_MASK) | CPUCLOCK_VIRT;
        // Tiny userspace bit-twiddle replaces string parsing. | ~3 uOps | near-zero energy compared with procfs path
    }
    return true;
}

static jlong user_thread_cpu_time(Thread *thread) {
    clockid_t clockid;
    bool success = get_thread_clockid(thread, &clockid, false);
    return success ? os::Linux::thread_cpu_time(clockid) : -1;
    // Published result: 11.186 us/op -> 0.279 us/op under the article's 16-thread setup.
}

@Benchmark
public void getCurrentThreadUserTime() throws Throwable {
    user = mxThreadBean.getCurrentThreadUserTime();
    // Microbenchmark entry point in the cloned repo; repeated reads amplify the syscall-path delta.
}

    Commit validation: The current local clone contains the optimized parse loop and the matching JMH benchmark class. The proof numbers come from the OpenJDK review thread for PR 15776.

    Functional explanation: This is a parser hot-path cleanup. Common specifiers like %s, %d, and width-prefixed forms stop paying the full parser cost.

    Why 10%+ is plausible: The published review numbers are well beyond that bar: StringFormat.stringFormat moved from 13.249 ns/op to 4.649 ns/op, widthStringFormat from 60.755 to 24.284, and widthStringIntFormat from 93.495 to 29.234.

    Published timing: 13.249 ns/op -> 4.649 ns/op, 60.755 ns/op -> 24.284 ns/op, and 93.495 ns/op -> 29.234 ns/op.

    Before vs after slowdown: the old parser path is about 185.0% slower on the simple stringFormat case and about 219.8% slower on the widthStringIntFormat case.

    Visual hotspot share in this partial: the generic parser block takes about 73.1% of the simplified bar before, versus about 40.4% after, a 32.7 point drop.

    What the flamegraph proves: before, even trivial specifiers still pay the generic parser cost; after, common one-character conversions stay on the fast path and only uncommon forms fall back. Functionally the formatted string is identical, but technically the parser does far less state-machine work.

    Before review benchmark

    Generic parser work on every specifier, even for the trivial shapes.

    After review benchmark

    Direct scan plus fast-path for valid single-character conversions.

    Prediction Signal

    Before signal: formatting repeatedly pays generic parser overhead on small format strings. After direction: direct scan plus common-case fast path. Predicted trace: span=formatter.parse top=indexOf,Conversion.isValid,parser.parse.

    Full Code Example With Inline uOps and mWh

    These uOps and mWh annotations are illustrative talk aids, not direct hardware measurements.

    static List<FormatString> parse(String s) {
    while (i < max) {
        int n = s.indexOf('%', i);
        // Scan directly for '%' and fast-path single-char conversions. | fewer parser states | lower control-flow overhead
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        if (Conversion.isValid(c)) {
            al.add(new FormatSpecifier(c));
            // Cheap path for common %s / %d / width cases. | less parser work
        } else {
            int off = parser.parse();
        }
    }
}
